source_text: Haereat ergo prudentis animo lectoris multum interesse inter ea quae a possibili veniunt, et ea quae a necessario; naturaliaque omnia necessariis applicet, voluntaria vero possibilibus; et quaestiones universas ab ea, qua coeperint, parte consummet. Quoniam si per utramque caeco iudicio vagetur; in innumeros per verba pene omnia praecipitatur errores; quod quoniam satis claruit, apparet te nimis omnino caligasse, qui collegisti: Quomodo potuit malum, quod nusquam erat, exoriri in opere Dei; ita etiam, iam quod erat, transiit naturaliter per opus Dei. Vide enim quo sis involutus errore: peccatum prima voluntate conceptum, quod a possibili venit, in necessaria dicis fuisse mutatum, ut quomodo potuit oriri motus animi liber, ita sine motu libero transiret in naturalium necessitatem. Sed intellege quoniam necessariorum auctor sit Deus. Si ergo hoc facit Deus in naturis, quod fecit animus in culpis, necesse est ut sic sit reus, quomodo et ille cuius arguit voluntatem. Immo magis; quanto enim est plus necessarium quam possibile, tanto scelestius est ingenerare quam usurpare peccatum. Quod licet rerum natura non capiat; tamen hic ostenderim, multo peiorem esse opinionem tuam de Deo, quam Manichaei. Illius enim Deum vel subita bella truncarunt; tuum vero antiqua et multiplicata crimina corruperunt. Ac per hoc non solum de quaestione dissentis a Catholicis, sed omnino de Deo; non ipsum colis, quem nos aequissimum, omnipotentissimum, inviolabilem in Trinitate veneramur. Ergo permeare non potuit per naturam res voluntatis; meritoque nos diximus, quia opus diaboli per opus Dei transire non sinitur. Opus enim diaboli hominisque mali peccatum est, quod in nullo potest sine liberae motu voluntatis existere. Quod opus et diabolo et homini a possibili venit et venit; opus autem Dei est natura, in qua non a possibili, sed a necessario subsistit homo; quae natura multis est temporibus sine voluntate, quoniam vis eius aetate certa sentitur. Quamdiu ergo est natura sine voluntate, opus Dei tantummodo est; et haec quod non fecerit, non potest habere peccatum. Irrefutabiliter ergo dictum est, quia per opus Dei opus diaboli transire non sinitur. Non minus autem falsum est quam profanum, quod dixisti: Opus operis Dei transit per opus Dei. Hoc est enim dicere: Peccat et Deus, quia peccavit homo, quem fecit Deus. Nam sicut nusquam est peccatum, nisi in opere hominis; neque enim cum peccaverit homo, aliquid substantiae eius additur, ut peccatum ibi eminere videatur, sed tantummodo malum opus de mala voluntate commissum, illi quoque a quo factum est, comparat meritum malum, ut malus dicatur qui mala fecit; ita etiam Deus tuus, si malum in opere suo fecit, nihil quidem substantiae eius accedit, sicut nec hominis; tamen meritum ei deformissimum comparatur, ut malus male faciendo dicatur. Parvulus sane probatur etiam tunc reus non esse, quia malitiam a necessario habet, quam nisi diabolus a possibili haberet, reus esse non posset. Deus autem qui verus est Christianorum, malum non facit; parvulus quoque ante propriae voluntatis arbitrium nihil habet, nisi quod in eo fecit Deus. Naturale igitur nullum esse peccatum potest. Sed quoniam sollicitissime antiqui erroris antra prorupimus, nec quidquam super hac quaestione occultum remansit; teneat lector diligens distinctionem necessarii atque possibilis; et non minus Manichaeorum, quam Traducianorum commenta ridebit.
pass_a_gloss: Let it therefore stick in the mind of a prudent reader that there is a great difference between those things which come from the possible and those which from the necessary; and let him apply all natural things to necessary, but voluntary things to possible; and let him consume all questions from that part from which they began. Because if he wanders through each by a blind judgment; he is precipitated into countless errors through almost all words; which since it has become sufficiently clear, it appears that you were altogether too much in a fog, you who gathered: How an evil which was nowhere could arise in a work of God; so also, what already was, passed naturally through a work of God. For see into what error you have been wrapped: a sin conceived by a first will, which comes from the possible, you say was changed into necessary things, so that as a free motion of the mind could arise, so without a free motion it would pass into a necessity of natural things. But understand that God is the author of necessary things. If therefore God does this in natures, which the mind did in faults, it is necessary that he be as guilty as that one whose will he accuses. Nay more; for as much as the necessary is more than the possible, so much more wicked is it to ingenerate than to usurp sin. Which although the nature of things does not take; nevertheless here I would have shown that your opinion about God is much worse than Manichaeus's. For sudden wars truncated that one's God; but ancient and multiplied charges corrupted yours. And through this you dissent not only about the question from the Catholics, but altogether about God; you do not worship him whom we venerate as most equitable, most omnipotent, inviolable in the Trinity. Therefore a thing of will could not permeate through nature; and deservedly we said that a work of the devil is not allowed to pass through a work of God. For a work of the devil and of an evil human is sin, which can exist in no one without a motion of a free will. Which work came and comes both to the devil and to the human from the possible; but a work of God is nature, in which the human subsists not from the possible but from the necessary; which nature is for many times without will, because its force is felt at a certain age. As long therefore as nature is without will, it is a work of God only; and this which it has not done cannot have sin. It has therefore been said irrefutably that a work of the devil is not allowed to pass through a work of God. But no less false than profane is what you said: A work of a work of God passes through a work of God. For this is to say: God also sins, because the human sinned, whom God made. For as sin is nowhere except in a work of the human; for neither when a human has sinned is something of his substance added, so that sin may seem to stand out there, but only an evil work committed from an evil will also furnishes an evil desert to him by whom it was made, so that he is called evil who did evil things; so also your God, if he made an evil in his work, nothing indeed of his substance accedes, as nor of the human's; yet a most deformed desert is furnished to him, so that he is called evil by doing evilly. A little one indeed is proved even then not to be guilty, because he has malice from the necessary, which unless the devil had from the possible, he could not be guilty. But God who is true of the Christians does not make evil; a little one also before the decision of his own will has nothing except what God made in him. There can therefore be no natural sin. But since we have most anxiously burst the caves of the ancient error, nor has anything remained hidden upon this question; let the diligent reader hold the distinction of the necessary and of the possible; and he will laugh at the inventions no less of the Manichaeans than of the Traducians.

pass_b_english: Let the discerning reader therefore hold firmly in mind the great difference between what comes from possibility and what comes from necessity. Let him assign all natural things to the necessary, all voluntary things to the possible, and conclude every question on the same side on which it began. If he wanders blindly through both, almost every word plunges him into countless errors. Since this has been made sufficiently clear, you plainly groped in deep darkness when you concluded: ‘Just as evil which existed nowhere could arise in God’s work, so evil already existing passed naturally through God’s work.’ See the error entangling you. You say sin conceived by the first will, which comes from possibility, was changed into something necessary: just as a free movement of the mind could arise, so without a free movement it could pass into the necessity of natural things.

Understand, however, that God is the author of necessary things. If God does in natures what the mind did in sins, he must be guilty in the same way as the one whose will he accuses. Indeed, more guilty: as necessity exceeds possibility, so engendering sin is more criminal than committing it. Although the nature of things does not admit this, I have shown here that your opinion of God is much worse than Mani’s. At least sudden wars mutilated Mani’s God; ancient and multiplied crimes corrupted yours. Consequently, you differ from catholics not merely over a question but over God himself. You do not worship the one whom we venerate in the Trinity as supremely just, supremely powerful, and inviolable.

A matter of will therefore could not pass through nature. We rightly said that the devil’s work is not permitted to pass through God’s work. The devil’s and an evil human being’s work is sin, which can exist in no one without a movement of free will. This work has come and comes to devil and human being from possibility. God’s work, however, is nature, in which a human being exists not by possibility but by necessity. This nature exists for long periods without will, since will’s power is felt at a particular age. As long as nature exists without will, it is solely God’s work; it cannot possess a sin it has not committed. It was therefore said irrefutably that the devil’s work is not permitted to pass through God’s work.

Your statement, ‘The work of God’s work passes through God’s work,’ is as false as it is impious. It amounts to saying, ‘God sins too, because the human being God made sinned.’ For sin exists nowhere except in a human being’s action. When a human being sins, nothing is added to his substance so that sin can be seen projecting there. The evil deed committed from an evil will simply acquires evil desert for the doer too, so that the one who did evil is called evil. Likewise, if your God made evil in his work, nothing is added to his substance, just as nothing is added to a human being’s; but he acquires the most disgraceful desert and is called evil by doing evil. Even then, however, the infant is proved not guilty, since he possesses evil by necessity, whereas even the devil could not be guilty unless he possessed it by possibility. But the true God of Christians does not do evil. Before the determination of its own will, an infant possesses nothing except what God has made within it. No natural sin can therefore exist. Since we have most carefully broken open the ancient error’s caves and nothing about this question remains hidden, let the attentive reader retain the distinction between necessity and possibility. He will laugh at the inventions of Manichaeans and advocates of inherited sin alike.

choices.why: Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)

choices.why: Glossary default: arbitrium is the decision-power, not a later Augustinian/Reformation free-will locus.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
